Optimizing SerDes Architecture for Advanced AI Workloads: Challenges and Solutions 
 
Phani Suresh Paladugu 
Synopsys, USA  
 
 
 
Abstract. The exponential growth of Artificial Intelligence applications makes sufficient 
demands on the high-performance computing infrastructure, with the Serializer/De-serializer 
(SERDES) interfaces, the memory system, and the data movement between the memory system 
and AI accelerator is emerging as a pivotal mediator, shaping the efficiency and performance 
of AI workloads. As AI models grow in scale and complexity, adapting high-speed interfaces 
becomes crucial for system performance across four key dimensions: bandwidth scalability, 
power efficiency, latency reduction, and signal integrity. Modern AI workloads operating on 
massive datasets demand terabit-per-second data transfer rates, while contending with stringent 
power consumption limits and communication latency challenges. Sophisticated modulation 
schemes, forward error correction, and channel bonding techniques unlock exceptional 
bandwidth potential, while cutting-edge circuit designs significantly lower energy 
consumption. Adaptive strategies—such as efficient encoding schemes and dedicated hardware 
paths—enable low-latency AI operations. At the same time, advanced equalization techniques 
and precise clocking systems preserve signal integrity at ultra-high data rates. The rapid 
demands of AI workloads call for ongoing innovation in interface architecture that goes beyond 
conventional adaptation methods, driving advancements at both the circuit and system levels. 
 
Keywords: SerDes architecture, Artificial Intelligence, bandwidth optimization, power 
efficiency, latency minimization, signal integrity

1. Introduction 
The rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications has placed unprecedented 
demands on high-performance computing infrastructure. The heart of these systems is the 
Serializer/De-Serializer interface, an important component that facilitates high-speed data 
transfer between the processor, memory system, and special AI accelerator. Since AI models 
continue to expand in size and complexity, Serdes customization has emerged as an important 
factor in determining the performance of the overall system. 
Modern AI workloads operate on massive datasets, often requiring data processing rates 
in the terabytes per second. According to Balasubramanian et al., training deep neural networks 
(DNNs) with 150–200 million parameters demands roughly 45 teraflops of compute power and 
memory bandwidth between 340 and 420 GB/s [2]. These models, however, represent only a 
small portion of today’s cutting-edge systems, which now feature trillions of parameters and 
even greater bandwidth demands. To support such performance, SerDes architectures must 
preserve signal integrity while functioning at frequencies above 28 GHz, even in channels 40–
100 cm long with losses reaching -20 dB at the Nyquist frequency. 
The SerDes design challenges go beyond achieving high bandwidth. Power consumption 
remains a critical constraint. Fares et al. report that high-speed SerDes operating at 25 Gbps 
can consume between 178 and 224 mW per lane, potentially contributing 18–22% of total 
system power in densely interconnected AI accelerator arrays [1]. This power demand is further 
intensified by the use of advanced equalization methods—continuous-time linear equalizers 
(CTLE) consume 32–48 mW, while decision feedback equalizers (DFE) add another 45–62 
mW in typical 28nm process implementations [1]. 
Latency poses a significant challenge, especially in distributed training scenarios. As 
highlighted in the hardware architecture tutorial by Sze et al., DNN training involves frequent 
weight updates that demand ultra-low communication latency, with optimal performance 
achieved when end-to-end latency stays below 10 ns [2]. Meeting these stringent latency targets 
while maintaining power efficiency requires careful optimization across the entire SerDes 
architecture. 
This paper investigates the specific demands placed on SerDes architectures by AI 
workloads and explores advanced optimization strategies to address these challenges. The 
analysis centers on four key performance dimensions: bandwidth scalability, power efficiency, 
latency reduction, and signal integrity. The rapid growth of AI workloads necessitates 
innovative interface design approaches that go beyond conventional adaptation techniques, 
driving advancements at both the circuit and architectural levels.

2. Bandwidth Optimization Techniques for AI Workloads 
The computational demands of modern AI workloads necessitate SerDes interfaces with 
unprecedented bandwidth capabilities. Training large language models and deep neural 
networks involves the continuous transfer of weights, activations, and gradients across system 
components. Sun et al. highlight that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) involve 
substantial data movement—for instance, VGGNet-16 requires a memory bandwidth of 15.5 
GB/s during inference and peaks at 393 MB of memory usage across convolutional layers [3]. 
Their study reveals that CNN memory access patterns resemble structured spatial terrains: a 
single 3×3 convolution window incurs nine operations per output activation, resulting in a 
compute-to-communication ratio of 9:1:1. This underscores the need for high-throughput 
interconnects to support such workloads. 
Modern SerDes architectures have evolved significantly, reaching data rates of 112 Gb/s 
and beyond—up from the 10–25 Gb/s typical in earlier generations. This leap has been enabled 
by several key innovations. Advanced modulation schemes like PAM-4 (Pulse Amplitude 
Modulation with 4 levels) effectively double the data rate compared to traditional NRZ (Non-
Return-to-Zero) signaling within the same Nyquist bandwidth. Jhong et al. demonstrated a 112 
Gb/s PAM-4 system capable of operating over channels with 33 dB insertion loss at the Nyquist 
frequency, achieving a fourfold improvement over comparable NRZ systems while 
maintaining bit error rates below 10⁻⁶ without additional error correction [4]. Forward Error 
Correction (FEC), once seen as too complex for high-speed SerDes, is now integral for reliable 
communication. Zhong et al. implemented a Reed-Solomon RS(528,514) FEC scheme that 
delivered a 2.7 dB coding gain and supported pre-FEC BERs of 2.4×10⁻⁴, enabling robust 
performance across lossy backplane channels. This implementation consumed only 17 mW at 
112 Gb/s and occupied 0.021 mm² in 7nm CMOS—just 6.8% of the total SerDes area [4]. 
In parallel, channel bonding strategies now enable multiple SerDes lanes to operate as a 
single, cohesive link, pushing aggregate throughput beyond 1 Tbps. Sun et al. investigated such 
approaches in FPGA-based CNN accelerators, finding that optimal bandwidth allocation across 
on-chip and off-chip channels can achieve up to 61.62 GOPS per DSP under a 19.2 GB/s 
bandwidth constraint [3]. These strategies are particularly relevant for edge devices constrained 
by thermal and power limitations. Emerging modulation formats like PAM-6 and PAM-8 are 
also under investigation for further bandwidth scaling. However, these formats present 
significant challenges in signal integrity and power efficiency. Thus, high-bandwidth interface 
design must strike a careful balance between raw throughput, energy efficiency, silicon area, 
and manufacturability.

3. Power Efficiency Enhancements in SerDes Design 
Power efficiency is a critical design consideration in SerDes interfaces targeting AI 
workloads, particularly within hyperscale data centers where energy consumption directly 
impacts operational cost and scalability. Modern SerDes architectures have achieved 
substantial improvements in power efficiency through holistic optimization strategies. Chan et 
al. present a 16nm CMOS SerDes design that operates at 25 Gb/s with a power efficiency of 
4.5 pJ/bit, enabled by a novel voltage-mode driver and advanced receiver equalization 
techniques [5]. Their breakdown of power consumption shows 42% allocated to receiver 
components, 28% to transmitter circuits, 18% to clock distribution, and 12% to support logic—
offering clear direction for targeted efficiency gains. 
Low-swing signaling techniques have become instrumental in reducing transmitter 
power, with recent implementations lowering voltage swings from 1V to sub-100mV levels. 
In Chan et al.'s design, a voltage-mode driver with programmable impedance control operates 
at 140mV swing, maintaining robust signal integrity over FR4 channels with 25 dB insertion 
loss at 12.5 GHz [5]. The design also features a 4-tap feed-forward equalizer, delivering up to 
30 dB of equalization at the Nyquist frequency while consuming only 24 mW—a 37% 
reduction compared to traditional current-mode logic solutions. 
Adaptive voltage scaling is another powerful technique, allowing real-time supply 
voltage adjustment across analog, clock, and digital blocks to match performance and channel 
requirements. Mahmood et al. developed a power management framework for high-speed 
SerDes interfaces that dynamically tunes voltage levels in 25 mV steps, achieving 22.8% power 
savings under typical conditions while maintaining bit error rates below 10⁻¹⁵. The system 
responds to changing channel states in under 115 µs, ensuring both adaptability and reliability 
[6]. 
Additional power-saving strategies include aggressive clock gating and adaptive 
equalization. Chan et al. implement clock gating on 85% of digital logic, achieving a 31% 
power reduction during link inactivity. Their architecture supports rapid link reactivation, 
completing training sequences in just 80 ns [5]. Meanwhile, Mahmood et al. employ an 
adaptive equalization scheme that tunes CTLE peaking (0–9 dB) and DFE tap weights based 
on real-time error feedback, lowering equalization power by 34% compared to static worst-
case settings [6]. Recent SerDes implementations have achieved power efficiencies as low as 
3-4 pJ/bit at 112 to 224 Gb/s—an order-of-magnitude improvement over previous generations. 
Achieving such efficiency requires system-wide optimization across all SerDes subsystems, 
including transmitters, receivers, clock generation circuits, and equalizers. These 
advancements must be realized without compromising signal integrity or introducing excessive 
implementation complexity.

4. Latency Minimization Strategies for Time-Critical AI Operations 
Latency in SerDes interfaces has become a critical factor for AI workloads, particularly 
in applications involving real-time inference or distributed training across multiple accelerator 
nodes. Both end-to-end and round-trip latencies directly affect key system-level performance 
metrics such as training duration and inference responsiveness. Zhu et al. report that 
communication latency accounts for 23–38% of total training time in large-scale AI systems, 
with SerDes links responsible for 15–27% of that latency bottleneck [7]. In their study of a 64-
node distributed training platform running a 1.3-billion-parameter transformer model, reducing 
SerDes latency from 6.2 ns to 3.8 ns led to an 11.6% increase in overall training throughput—
emphasizing the importance of interconnect optimization in high-performance AI 
infrastructure. 
Modern SerDes designs incorporate multiple latency-minimizing strategies without 
compromising power efficiency or signal integrity. Innovations in clock and data recovery 
(CDR) architectures—especially those targeting burst-mode traffic—are significantly reducing 
acquisition and lock times. Zhou et al. introduce an all-digital CDR system that achieves 
frequency lock in just 38 clock cycles (approximately 1.52 ns at 25 Gb/s), followed by phase 
alignment within an additional 15–20 cycles (600–800 ps) [8]. Their dual-stage acquisition 
technique, combining coarse frequency detection with fine phase correction, maintains bit error 
rates below 10⁻¹² and supports jitter tolerance of 0.31 UI at 10 MHz, all across a wide 
temperature range (0°C to 85°C). 
Lightweight encoding schemes further reduce latency by minimizing serialization 
overhead. Zhu et al. develop an AI-optimized encoding protocol that reduces the overhead of 
traditional 64b/66b schemes by 27% through tailored design for structured AI data patterns [7]. 
Their encoder achieves sub-112 ps latency while preserving adequate transition density for 
robust clock recovery—an important tradeoff in minimizing protocol-induced delays. Forward 
error correction (FEC) schemes are also being optimized for low-latency applications. Zhou et 
al. implement a CRC-16-based detection mechanism that adds only 240 ps of latency while 
detecting up to 99.997% of multi-bit errors in 25 Gb/s transmission scenarios [8]. The design 
consumes just 0.006 mm² in 28nm CMOS, offering efficient resource usage while meeting 
stringent timing constraints. 
Architectural enhancements such as intelligent buffer management and priority-based 
flow control also play a key role in latency reduction. Zhu et al. demonstrate a SerDes 
architecture with dedicated low-latency paths for control signaling that bypass conventional 
buffering mechanisms, reducing control signal latency to 0.86 ns—compared to 3.2 ns via 
standard data paths [7]. Additionally, research into asynchronous SerDes architectures, which 
decouple transmission from strict clock-domain constraints, shows potential for further latency 
reductions. State-of-the-art SerDes interfaces are now capable of achieving latencies under a 
few nanoseconds across chip-to-chip links—enabling real-time communication between 
distributed AI processing nodes and significantly accelerating model convergence and 
inference performance.

5. Signal Integrity and Reliability in High-Performance AI Systems 
Signal integrity and reliability are foundational requirements for SerDes interfaces in AI 
systems, where even minor data corruption can lead to model convergence issues, erroneous 
inference outputs, or system-level failures. As data rates continue to rise, maintaining ultra-low 
bit error rates (BER)—typically targeted at 10⁻¹⁵ or lower—has become increasingly difficult. 
Ahmed et al. highlight that at data rates exceeding 56 Gb/s, maintaining acceptable channel 
loss requires advanced equalization techniques, particularly for standard backplane channels 
which exhibit 28–35 dB insertion loss at the Nyquist frequency [9]. Their study of high-speed 
interconnects in AI accelerators shows that frequency-dependent losses in FR4-based PCBs 
reach 0.7–0.8 dB/inch at 14 GHz, with additional loss from vias and connectors contributing 
1.2–1.8 dB per transition—posing serious equalization challenges for SerDes systems. 
To address these challenges, modern SerDes designs employ sophisticated equalization 
strategies across multiple domains. Advanced techniques compensate for channel impairments 
such as high-frequency attenuation, reflections, and inter-symbol interference. Adaptive 
equalizers dynamically tune parameters to match changing conditions. Liu et al. demonstrate a 
112 Gb/s PAM-4 SerDes implementation that integrates a comprehensive equalization chain: 
a 5-tap Feed-Forward Equalizer (FFE) at the transmitter, a 3-stage Continuous-Time Linear 
Equalizer (CTLE) with programmable peaking from 0 to 14 dB, and a 7-tap Decision Feedback 
Equalizer (DFE) at the receiver [10]. Their system maintains reliable operation over channels 
with up to 38 dB insertion loss at 28 GHz, achieving pre-FEC BERs below 2.4×10⁻⁶ and post-
FEC BERs below 10⁻¹⁵. 
The combined use of DFE, FFE, and CTLE forms a robust hybrid equalization 
architecture. Ahmed et al. evaluate this approach, showing that the integrated use of these 
techniques yields an additional 4.2–5.7 dB margin compared to any single method applied in 
isolation [9]. Their measurements reveal that CTLE typically compensates for 6–8 dB of loss, 
FFE contributes 4–7 dB, and DFE adds 5–9 dB—together enabling reliable performance in 
channels previously considered too lossy for high-speed transmission. 
Signal integrity also hinges on precise clock generation and distribution to minimize 
jitter. Liu et al. implement an LC-tank-based clock generator with phase noise of -110 dBc/Hz 
at a 1 MHz offset from a 14 GHz carrier, achieving an integrated RMS jitter of just 157 fs [10]. 
Their design incorporates digital supply regulation to limit voltage ripple to below 3.2 mV

At the receiver, advanced clock and data recovery (CDR) circuits enhance jitter tolerance 
and phase tracking capabilities. Comprehensive link training procedures initialize optimal 
parameters during startup, while continuous background calibration adapts to environmental 
variations over time. These combined innovations make it possible to sustain reliable high-
speed data transmission—such as 112-224 Gb/s PAM-4 signaling—under conditions where 
conventional approaches would fail. 
 
Conclusion 
The evolution of SerDes technology is closely intertwined with advancements in artificial 
intelligence, forming a symbiotic relationship in which improvements in data communication 
directly enhance computational performance. AI workloads place increasingly demanding 
requirements on SerDes interfaces across multiple dimensions, including bandwidth 
scalability, power efficiency, latency reduction, and adaptability—all while maintaining 
stringent signal integrity. Modern SerDes implementations have made significant strides, with 
single-lane data rates now reaching 112–224 Gb/s, energy efficiencies of 3–4 pJ/bit, end-to-
end latencies under few nanoseconds, and reliable performance even under challenging channel 
conditions. These achievements are the result of sophisticated engineering solutions that 
integrate advanced modulation formats, adaptive equalization techniques, low-overhead 
encoding schemes, and high-precision timing architectures. As AI systems continue to scale in 
complexity and performance, future SerDes innovations will likely involve cutting-edge 
technologies such as photonic interconnects, novel modulation strategies, and AI-optimized 
communication architectures tailored to specific data movement patterns. With AI demanding 
ever-higher throughput and responsiveness, SerDes performance remains a critical determinant 
of overall system scalability, energy efficiency, and computational throughput.
